title: The First Years
note: Management Executive and Senior Management Executive (ranks 0-1), which every graduate and poly career passes through, and where a poly entrant can still be in their fifties: nothing here assumes a new or young officer. The run's peer, senior and junior carry the stories. and_team names the peer by what an earlier card remembers (the_work's slides, the post-it workshop's "agree"). Three callbacks pay off years later: copied_in_file and copied_in_repaid follow the peer you did or did not warn, and for_the_record_audit finds the notes you kept.

events.title: One Word

topic.text: why the renewal form asks for the same date three times
whether to extend a pilot by a year

word.a: Your second version is better, and goes up on Thursday. It comes back with the same word. You learn, eventually, that "Discuss" was never about the paper. It meant: come upstairs and talk to me.
word.b: {senior} reads the paper while you wait, agrees with all four pages, and tells you to send it on as it is. That was the discussion. It took six minutes.
word.c: Your reply says: "Happy to discuss." It comes back: "Discuss." The paper goes back and forth between your desk and {senior}'s three more times before either of you books a meeting room.

word.a: The new version opens with the answer to "Why?" in one paragraph. {senior} reads that paragraph, approves the paper, and returns the other three pages unread.
word.b: {senior} explains that "Why?" meant "why now?": the answer depends on a budget cycle you haven't heard of yet. You write that down, and add a paragraph about it.
word.c: Your reply is one line long, and answers the question. {senior} writes "OK" beneath it. You keep the page in a drawer for years, for no reason you could explain.

word.a: Four pages become two. The new version also comes back marked "Noted." You learn that it means read, agreed with, and not to be acted on this financial year.
word.b: {senior} is surprised to see you, and explains kindly that "Noted" is a complete reply. It means the paper was read. It does not mean anything will happen, and nothing does.
word.c: Your reply asks what happens next, and comes back marked "Noted." as well. Eighteen months later someone else finds your paper in a file, sends it up again, and it is approved.

word.a: You rewrite it before going up, to be safe. {senior} only wanted to say it was good. There are now two good versions, and a meeting about which one to use.
word.b: You go up at once. {senior} wanted to say it was good, and to put a face to the paper. The meeting takes four minutes. You replay it for a week.
word.c: Your reply says you are free all afternoon. {senior} is not. The meeting happens three weeks later, by which time the paper has gone up anyway, unchanged.

word.a: Four pages become one. {senior} approves it and sends it upstairs, where the next reader writes "Pls elaborate" across the top.
word.b: {senior} explains that the paper is fine, but the person it goes to next reads everything on a phone, in a car, between meetings. You learn to write for the car.
word.c: Your one-line reply reads, in full: "Noted." It is the shortest thing you have ever sent upstairs, and {senior} approves the paper on the strength of it.

events.body: You spent a week on a minute paper for {senior}, your reporting officer, on {topic}. It runs to four pages, and it's the first paper of yours meant to go further upstairs. It comes back the next morning with one word in the margin, in {senior}'s handwriting: "{word}"

choices.text: Rewrite it from the top.
choices.outcome: {word.a}

choices.text: Go up and ask {senior} what the word means.
choices.outcome: {word.b}

choices.text: Send it back up unchanged, with a one-line reply.
choices.outcome: {word.c}

events.title: Friday, 5pm

owner.a: On Monday the Permanent Secretary's PA writes to ask, politely, about a yoghurt. Your reply quotes paragraph 3. The circular is reissued the following week, with a new paragraph 4, on exemptions.
owner.b: The yoghurt survives six more Fridays while everyone else's lunch goes in the bin. The floor draws its own conclusion about who paragraph 3 applies to, and shares it at the pantry sink, while you're there.
owner.c: The Permanent Secretary replies to all forty of you: "Mine. Pls bin. Thanks for checking." It becomes the most forwarded email on the floor that year, and the friendliest.

owner.text: with a smiley face and the name of {peer}
owner.a: {peer} finds the empty shelf on Monday, laughs, and pins a copy of the circular to the fridge door with paragraph 3 highlighted and your initials in the margin.
owner.b: You bin everyone's food but {peer}'s. Nobody says anything. On Monday morning somebody has labelled the milk, the butter and the chilli sauce with {peer}'s name too.
owner.c: Forty people now know that {peer} keeps a yoghurt for eleven days. {peer} collects it from your desk in person, to applause, and bins it.

owner.text: "DO NOT THROW", in capitals, and nothing else
owner.a: You bin it. On Monday a new yoghurt appears, labelled "DO NOT THROW. I MEAN IT." You bin that one on Friday too. Neither of you gives up before the quarter ends.
owner.b: The yoghurt stays. By March it has outlasted two office managers and the fridge's thermostat, and the floor calls it, without irony, "the tenant".
owner.c: Nobody claims it. Three people reply to say it is not theirs, and one to ask what paragraph 3 says. At 5pm it goes into the bin anyway.

events.body: The office pantry fridge is cleared at 5pm every Friday, under paragraph 3 of an office circular: anything past its date goes in the bin. This quarter, the clearing is your job. Behind the milk sits a yoghurt, eleven days past its date, labelled {owner}.

choices.text: Bin it, as paragraph 3 says.
choices.outcome: {owner.a}

choices.text: Clear everything else, and leave the yoghurt.
choices.outcome: {owner.b}

choices.text: Email the floor, asking the owner to claim it.
choices.outcome: {owner.c}

events.title: And Team

options.text: {peer}, whose half of the slides you once presented as your own,
{peer}, who once put "agree" beside your post-it,

events.body: You and {with} spent a month on a {doc}. Your reporting officer, {senior}, sends it up to the Deputy Secretary under {senior.their} own name only. The Deputy Secretary's reply thanks {senior} "and team". {peer} forwards it to you without comment, clearly annoyed.

choices.text: Ask {senior} to put all three names on the next one.
choices.outcome: {senior} agrees at once, and seems surprised you had to ask. The next {doc} goes up with three names on it, and the Deputy Secretary's reply thanks "the team". You decide to count that.

choices.text: Reply to the Deputy Secretary, and name who did the work.
choices.outcome: Your reply is two lines long and names {peer} first. The Deputy Secretary answers, "Well done, both." {senior} leaves you off every email for three months, then copies you on everything.

choices.text: Say nothing. Papers go up under your reporting officer's name.
choices.outcome: You build the next {doc} too, and it also goes up under {senior}'s name. In March {senior} is promoted, and asks for you to move with {senior.them}. {peer} isn't asked.

events.title: Copied In

above.text: a Deputy Secretary and two directors
the HR director and the Chief Information Officer
a Permanent Secretary, and nobody else

events.body: An email arrives that clearly wasn't meant for you. You're copied in, below {above}, on a confidential plan for next year's restructuring, marked Official (Closed). Paragraph two abolishes the job of {peer}, who joined the service with you. {peer} doesn't know yet.

choices.text: Tell {peer}, quietly, after work.
choices.outcome: Over kopi, without mentioning any email, you tell {peer} it might be a good time to look around. {peer} applies for two other jobs that week, gets one, and never asks how you knew.

choices.text: Say nothing. It wasn't sent to you to share.
choices.outcome: The restructuring is announced six weeks later at a townhall. {peer} hears it with everyone else and is moved to another job in good order. You say all the right things, a little too smoothly for someone hearing it for the first time.

choices.text: Tell the sender you were copied in by mistake.
choices.outcome: {above.office} thanks you in one line and takes you off the list. Nobody ever says who added you. For a while you open every email expecting to be on it.

events.title: The Cc Line
events.body: Years ago you were copied in, by mistake, on a confidential plan that abolished the job of {peer}, and you said nothing. Now {peer}, looking for something else in an old file, has found that email. It is dated six weeks before anyone told {peer.them}, and your name is on the cc line.

choices.text: Explain, properly, over kopi.
choices.outcome: You explain: the email was marked Official (Closed), it wasn't yours to share, and you hated keeping quiet for six weeks. {peer} hears you out and says {peer.they} would have done the same. Neither of you is sure that's true.

choices.text: Point out that it was marked Official (Closed).
choices.outcome: {peer} agrees that it was. The conversation is short and entirely correct. For years afterwards {peer} is perfectly cordial to you in every meeting, and says nothing to you at all in the lift.

events.title: Face Down
events.body: A few years ago, you quietly warned {peer} that a restructuring would abolish {peer.their} job. Today {peer} closes your door and puts a printout on your desk, face down: next year's postings, which nobody is meant to see until April. "You told me once," {peer} says.

choices.text: Turn it over.
choices.outcome: Your name is on it: you're being posted somewhere difficult in April. With three months' notice you ask for that posting yourself, so it looks like your idea. Nobody upstairs ever learns that you knew first.

choices.text: Leave it face down, and thank {peer}.
choices.outcome: {peer} takes the printout back without a word, and looks almost relieved. In April the postings come out. Yours is somewhere difficult, and you are the only person on the floor who is surprised.

events.title: For the Record

line.text: that the project will not meet its target this year or next
line.why: if it's in the minutes, someone will one day ask why nobody acted on it

line.text: that the new system will miss its launch date, and that the date will not be moved
line.why: if it's in the minutes, someone will one day ask why it launched anyway

line.text: that the vendor building it has already failed two other agencies the same way
line.why: if it's in the minutes, someone will one day ask why the ministry hired them anyway

events.body: You're taking the minutes at a meeting between {speaker} and three agencies about a project that is already behind. Forty minutes in, {speaker} says, calmly, {line}. Nobody wants that in writing: {line.why}. You write the draft, and {speaker.approver} approves it before it goes out.

choices.text: Minute it exactly as it was said.
choices.outcome: The minutes go out with the line in paragraph six, word for word. Nobody replies. Two weeks later you're taken off the meeting's mailing list, and then off the meeting.

choices.text: Leave it out, and minute only the decisions.
choices.outcome: Your minutes say "The meeting noted the challenges ahead." They're approved in one round, unchanged: the first thing you've written that went upstairs without a single edit.

choices.text: Minute it, and point it out to {speaker.approver} when you send the draft.
choices.outcome: The draft comes back with the line crossed out and initialled. The crossed-out draft is filed next to the final minutes, as drafts always are, where anyone who looks can read both.

events.title: The Note-Taker

options.text: your minutes, with the warning in paragraph six
your draft of the minutes, with the warning crossed out and initialled

events.body: Years ago, in your first years in the service, you took the minutes at a meeting where someone senior warned, calmly, that a project would go wrong. It did. The Auditor-General's Office is now auditing it, and the only written record of that warning is {record}. The auditors would like to speak to whoever took the notes.

choices.text: Confirm the record, and that you wrote it.
choices.outcome: The audit report quotes your minutes in a footnote, without your name. Everyone who was at that meeting knows who took them, and two of them tell you so: one to thank you, and one not.

choices.text: Confirm it's accurate, and say nothing more.
choices.outcome: You confirm the record is accurate and add nothing. The footnote appears anyway. What the people in it remember is that you didn't help them either.

events.title: The Lucky Draw

prize.text: an air fryer, for the third year running

events.body: You missed the meeting where the D&D committee was picked, so you're on it. The theme is {theme}. The top prize is {prize}, and the box for the lucky draw holds every name in the division, directors included.

choices.text: Draw it straight, whoever comes out.
choices.outcome: The Permanent Secretary wins it, and gives it back to be drawn again, to applause. So does a director, and then another. By the fourth draw, the prize has been on stage longer than the band.

choices.text: Quietly take the directors' names out first.
choices.outcome: An officer in her first month wins it, and cries a little. The directors, spared the business of giving it back, are quietly grateful. Nobody ever checks the box.

choices.text: Spend the prize money on the food instead.
choices.outcome: The food is the best anyone can remember, and there's no lucky draw. Next year a third fewer people come. It turns out nobody came for the food.

events.title: The Internet Laptop
events.body: A vendor has sent {file} as a download link, and {senior}, your reporting officer, wants it by 2pm. Your work laptop can't open the link: government work laptops are kept off the internet, for security. The division's one internet laptop is booked until 3pm. There is a quick way round this, and it breaks the IT rules.

choices.text: Open it on your phone and email it to your work account.
choices.outcome: {senior} has it at 1:52pm. Three months later the IT security review finds your email, and you're sent on a forty-minute refresher course on the government's IT rules, with a quiz at the end and a certificate.

choices.text: Ask the vendor to email it as an attachment instead.
choices.outcome: The vendor emails it as one attachment, which bounces for being too large, then as six, one of which the virus scanner quarantines. {senior} gets it on Thursday, two days late, and asks what happened.

choices.text: Read it on your phone, and retype it.
choices.outcome: Six pages, retyped by 1:58pm, with two typos, both in the vendor's name. Every keystroke was compliant. When you explain how you did it, nobody believes you.

events.title: Station 4

exhibit.text: a poster of the new scheme
a tablet running the new app
a service counter, repainted for the visit

events.body: The Minister is visiting your division, and the visit is planned to the minute. You're at Station 4, beside {exhibit}, from 10:42 to 10:45am. Your reporting officer, {senior}, is two steps behind the Minister. At 10:43 the Minister turns to you and asks whether it actually works. It doesn't, yet.

choices.text: Say "not yet, Minister", and why.
choices.outcome: The Minister asks a second question that isn't on the plan, then a third. The visit leaves Station 4 four minutes late. {senior} never mentions it to you.

choices.text: Give the answer from the briefing notes.
choices.outcome: "It's progressing well, Minister." The visit moves on to Station 5 at 10:45 exactly. That evening {senior} sends you a thumbs-up, the first one ever. You keep it.

choices.text: Say what would make it work, in ninety seconds.
choices.outcome: The Minister's private secretary writes it down. To make up the time, Station 5 is dropped from the visit, and the officer at Station 5, who rehearsed for a week, finds you at lunch to tell you so.

events.title: Standard Operating Procedure
events.body: {junior} has just joined your section, and has been handed the official standard operating procedures: forty-one pages, last updated two reorganisations ago, and mostly out of date. You keep your own version on one page of a notebook. It's the reason you get things done faster than anyone else on the floor.

choices.text: Give {junior} your page.
choices.outcome: Your page says which director reads only the first paragraph, which printer jams, and who in HR picks up before nine. {junior} is useful within a week, and photocopies it.

choices.text: Let {junior} learn it the way you did.
choices.outcome: {junior} learns it by getting it wrong in front of the right people. It takes a year. Neither of you mentions it, and {junior} starts a notebook.

choices.text: Rewrite the forty-one pages around your one.
choices.outcome: It takes three months of evenings. The division adopts your new procedures, with your name in the version history and nowhere else, and {junior} learns them in a weekend.

events.title: Approved Leave

away.text: a hotel lobby in Seattle, at 1:40am local time
a hotel room in New York, at 4:40am local time
a beach bar in Honolulu, at 10:40pm the evening before

events.body: In January, {senior} approved your two weeks' leave for September, and you booked your flights. Now {senior} has moved the division's Work Plan Seminar, where each section presents next year's plans, into the second week of your leave. This year's theme is Staff Well-being, and nobody else can present your section's slide.

choices.text: Cancel the leave and present the slide.
choices.outcome: You cancel the trip. Your slide, "Rest as a Strategic Enabler", is on at 4:40pm, and the Deputy Secretary leaves at 4:42. The airline gives you a voucher instead of a refund, and it expires unused, like the leave.

choices.text: Go. Someone else can present it.
choices.outcome: {senior} presents your slide for you, and tells the room you are "role-modelling the theme". Two directors write that down. You come back rested, and do the best work of your year.

choices.text: Present it by video, from the holiday.
choices.outcome: From {away}, you present the slide on Staff Well-being. The connection holds. Three directors say how good it was to see you. Nobody mentions the slide.
